sections.content:
## What You'll Learn

By the end of this lesson you'll understand how every file on your computer is organized, what a file path actually means, and why this matters the moment you start working with code. None of this is complicated — it's just a mental model most people never get taught explicitly.

## The File System Is a Tree

Your computer organizes all its files in a **hierarchy** — think of it as an upside-down tree. At the very top (the root) is a drive, typically `C:\` on Windows. Every folder on your computer is a branch off that root, and every file is a leaf at the end of a branch.

Here's what that looks like:

```
C:\
├── Users\
│   └── Alice\
│       ├── Documents\
│       │   ├── Work\
│       │   └── Personal\
│       └── Desktop\
└── Program Files\
```

This structure — folders inside folders inside folders — is called a **directory tree**. The terms *folder* and *directory* mean the same thing; older documentation uses *directory*, modern interfaces use *folder*.

**Drives** are the top-level containers. Most Windows computers have one main drive called `C:`. If you plug in a USB stick or external hard drive, Windows assigns it another letter like `D:` or `E:`. The colon after the letter is how Windows signals "this is a drive." Everything starts from here.

## Anatomy of a File

Every file has four things that define it:

**Name** — The human-readable label, like `report` or `photo`.

**Extension** — The two-to-four letters after the dot that tell your computer *what kind of file this is*: `.txt` means plain text, `.jpg` means a photo, `.html` means a webpage, `.py` means a Python script. The extension is how Windows knows which program to open when you double-click a file.

**Path** — The full address of the file in the directory tree. More on this below.

**Icon** — The visual shortcut your computer uses to represent the file type. The icon is generated from the extension — it isn't stored in the file itself.

By default, Windows *hides* file extensions. This means `resume.docx` appears as just `resume`. This is unhelpful when you're learning to code, because the extension is crucial. Lesson 4-2 covers how to show extensions permanently.

## Paths: The Address of a File

A **path** is the full address that tells your computer exactly where a file lives. There are two types:

**Absolute path** — starts from the root of the drive and gives the complete location of a file, no matter where you currently are:
```
C:\Users\Alice\Documents\Work\report.docx
```
This is unambiguous. It will find the file from anywhere on the computer.

**Relative path** — describes a location *relative to where you currently are*. If you're already inside `C:\Users\Alice\Documents`, then the relative path to the same file is just:
```
Work\report.docx
```

Think of the difference this way: an **absolute path** is like a GPS address — it works from anywhere. A **relative path** is like saying "turn left, then the second door on the right" — it only makes sense if you already know where you're starting from.

**The backslash `\`** separates folders on Windows. You'll also see forward slashes `/` — that's the convention on Mac and Linux. Many tools accept either.

**The key insight for coding:** Code files are just files. When you write a program, you're creating text files in a folder. When that code references another file (an image, a stylesheet, a database), it uses a path to find it. If you get the path wrong, the file doesn't load. Understanding paths is not optional — it's one of the most practical skills in this entire course.

sections.title: Draw Your File Tree
sections.content:
Open Notepad (or any notes app) and draw the folder structure of your Documents folder as a tree. Follow this pattern:

```
Documents\
├── [Folder 1]\
│   ├── [Subfolder]\
│   └── [Another subfolder]\
├── [Folder 2]\
└── [Folder 3]\
    └── [File inside it]
```

Don't worry about getting every folder — just the ones you actually use and recognise.

Then, write the **absolute path** to one specific file inside your Documents folder. It should look something like:
```
C:\Users\YourName\Documents\SomeFolder\SomeFile.docx
```

Finally, write one sentence answering: *"Why does a coder need to understand file paths?"*

Save this — it's the foundation everything in Parts 4 and 5 builds on.

sections.question: What is the difference between an absolute path and a relative path?
options: An absolute path starts from the drive root and works from anywhere; a relative path describes a location from where you currently are
An absolute path uses backslashes; a relative path uses forward slashes
An absolute path is for files; a relative path is for folders
An absolute path is longer; a relative path is shorter
sections.explanation: An absolute path always starts from the root (like C:\) and unambiguously identifies a file from anywhere on the computer. A relative path only makes sense in the context of a current location — it describes how to get to a file from where you already are.

sections.title: Workshop A — Quick Drill: Path Detective
sections.content:
5-minute drill to build path-reading fluency. No setup required.

1. Open File Explorer (Win+E).
2. Click in the address bar — note the full path displayed (e.g. C:\Users\YourName\Documents).
3. Navigate to three different locations and write the full absolute path for each:
   - Your Desktop
   - Your Downloads folder
   - Any subfolder inside Documents
4. For each path, identify: the drive letter, each folder name separated by backslashes, and the final destination.
5. Now pick one of those locations and write the relative path from your user home folder (C:\Users\YourName) to that location — just the part after the home folder.
6. Ask AI to check: paste your three absolute paths and one relative path to Claude and say: "I'm learning about file paths. Are these paths correctly formatted? Is my relative path correct relative to C:\Users\YourName?"
7. Fix any issues Claude identifies before moving on.

sections.title: Workshop B — Build It With AI: Your Personal File Map
sections.content:
Use Claude.ai to help you create a real organized file map of your computer. This produces a document you'll actually use.

1. Open Claude.ai in your browser.
2. Send this prompt: "I'm learning about file systems and paths. Help me design a clean folder structure for someone who works with [describe your job or main activities briefly]. I want folders for work projects, learning resources, and personal files. Give me the structure as a tree diagram with explanations for each top-level folder."
3. Read Claude's suggested structure. Note what you'd keep, remove, or rename.
4. Send a follow-up: "Now give me that same structure as a list of absolute Windows paths starting from C:\Users\YourName\, where each path ends in a backslash."
5. Open Notepad and paste the list of paths Claude gave you.
6. Add a column next to each path: write one sentence explaining what files would go in that folder.
7. Pick one path from the list. Ask Claude: "If I'm currently at C:\Users\YourName and I want to navigate to [paste your chosen path], what is the relative path I would use?"
8. Verify Claude's answer by thinking through it step by step — does each folder name in the relative path make sense?
9. Save your document as file-system-map.txt on your Desktop.
10. AI REVIEW step: Share your file-system-map.txt with Claude and say: "Review this file organization plan. Find 3 things wrong or that could be improved. Don't say it looks good." Fix at least one issue Claude identifies.
11. Keep this file — you'll use it to set up your actual folder structure in the next lesson.

sections.title: Workshop C — AI-Assisted Troubleshooting: Break a Path
sections.content:
Practice diagnosing path errors — the most common beginner mistake in all of coding.

1. Open Notepad.
2. Write these five deliberately broken paths:
   - `C:UsersAliceDocuments` (missing backslashes)
   - `C:\Users\Alice\Document` (misspelled folder name)
   - `Users\Alice\Documents\file.txt` (relative path pretending to be absolute)
   - `C:\Users\Alice\Documents\` (valid folder path, but what if you need a file?)
   - `C:/Users/Alice/Documents/file.txt` (forward slashes — valid on some tools, not all)
3. Try to open File Explorer and navigate to each broken path by clicking in the address bar and typing it. Observe what Windows says.
4. Paste all five broken paths to Claude with this message: "These are file paths I'm experimenting with on Windows. For each one: is it valid? If broken, explain exactly what's wrong and give me the corrected version."
5. Compare Claude's explanations to what you observed in File Explorer.
6. Write one sentence for each path: what the error was and why it matters in real coding.

sections.title: Workshop D — Real-World Application: Organize One Real Folder
sections.content:
Apply file organization knowledge to something you actually use.

1. Think of one folder on your computer that is genuinely messy or disorganized — Downloads, Desktop, or a work project folder are common candidates.
2. Open File Explorer and navigate to that folder.
3. Take a screenshot or write down what's in it (roughly — no need to list every file).
4. Open Claude.ai and describe the mess: "I have a folder called [name] that contains [describe roughly what's in it — documents, images, old downloads, etc.]. Help me design a subfolder structure to organize it. Give me specific folder names and explain what goes where."
5. Claude will suggest a structure. Ask a follow-up: "Give me the Windows paths for creating each of those subfolders, starting from [paste your current folder path]."
6. In File Explorer, right-click in the messy folder and create at least three of the subfolders Claude suggested.
7. Move at least five files into their correct new subfolders.
8. Write the absolute path of two files you moved — one before and one after. Example: `C:\Users\Alice\Downloads\report.pdf` became `C:\Users\Alice\Documents\Work\2026\report.pdf`.
9. Note: this real folder is now more organized, and you practiced absolute paths in a real context.

sections.question: A web developer has an image file at C:\projects\website\images\logo.png. Their HTML file is at C:\projects\website\index.html. What is the correct relative path to reference the image from the HTML file?
sections.explanation: Since both the HTML file and the images folder are in the same parent folder (website), the relative path from index.html to logo.png is simply images/logo.png — go into the images folder, then the file. The absolute path (option A) works but is bad practice in web development because it breaks when the project is moved. Option C (../images/logo.png) would go UP one level first, which is wrong since we're already in website/. Option D (logo.png) would only work if the image were in the same folder as the HTML file.

sections.question: You're troubleshooting why a Python script can't find a file it's trying to read. The script is in C:\projects\myapp\ and it references the file as 'data/users.csv'. Where must the file actually exist for this to work?
sections.explanation: When a script uses a relative path like data/users.csv, the path is relative to the script's location (or more precisely, the working directory when the script runs — usually the script's folder). So from C:\projects\myapp\, the path data/users.csv resolves to C:\projects\myapp\data\users.csv. This is one of the most common beginner errors: the file exists somewhere on the computer, but not at the relative path the code expects.

sections.content: **You've completed lesson 4-1.** You understand the file system tree, the anatomy of a file, absolute vs relative paths, and you've applied this to a real folder on your computer. In the next lesson you'll master File Explorer and copy paths directly from Windows.
